title: The Harbor That Listened
summary: Jun finally gets the opening solo at Sable Quay’s music festival. When she and Edda, a hard-of-hearing poster artist, collect the market’s sounds, a bread board and a very inconvenient hat make them rethink who gets to give the first beat.
coverAlt: Under the title The Harbor That Listened, Jun hugs a sketchbook decorated with rhythmic shapes. Edda lifts one hand toward the sea. A red rosette hangs against the pennant line, and stepped market roofs and sailboats curve around the blue harbor.
style: Coastal risograph in ultramarine, marigold, vermilion and warm paper, with brush-drawn silhouettes and two panoramic panels per page.

pages.alt: The wide-hatted festival host pins a red rosette to Jun’s striped sailor shirt at the crescent market. Under a row of pennants, Jun bends toward her knocking knees and the host smiles.
pages.transcript:
JUN
My first opening solo. Do I get the ribbon even if my knees knock?

HOST
Especially then. The ribbon likes a little rhythm.

pages.alt: Jun spreads her arms at Edda’s poster stall. At the worktable, the white-haired artist looks from her pencil and paper to Jun.
pages.transcript:
JUN
Edda, will you draw me a poster? Just me and a very large note.

EDDA
I’ll draw you a whole song. I’m hard of hearing. What does yours look like?

pages.alt: A baker pats a round loaf in front of Jun and Edda. Jun shows the baker two small dots and a big circle drawn in her sketchbook.
pages.transcript:
BAKER
Two light pats, one fat pat. That’s how a loaf says good morning.

JUN
Two crumbs and a bun. I can draw that!

pages.alt: A button seller tips her tin as Jun leans close. Overhead, the buttons settle into a crescent against the rim and Edda traces the open space.
pages.transcript:
BUTTON SELLER
Everyone talks about the lid. I like what comes after.

EDDA
I like that, too. The buttons lie down. The quiet has a shape.

pages.alt: The post clerk squares a stack of envelopes with a brisk motion. Jun and Edda compare its sharp corners to the round shapes in their book.
pages.transcript:
POST CLERK
The envelopes get one good snap. Then they behave until lunchtime.

JUN
That sound has corners. Edda, put it beside the bun.

pages.alt: Edda spreads a triangular yellow pennant across her worktable as Jun leans in. Out in the square, Edda raises an open hand in front of Jun, a child and the waiting drummers.
pages.transcript:
EDDA
You’ve gathered everyone’s sounds. What about my verse?

JUN
You want a whole bar with nothing in it?

pages.alt: Edda raises a hand in front of the waiting neighbors. Jun crouches beside a child at the back, where an enormous blue hat fills their view.
pages.transcript:
EDDA
Nothing? Look at the way they wait.

CHILD
I’m trying. From back here all I can see is Mr. Pel’s hat.

pages.alt: The broad-hatted host offers Jun the high step in the middle of the square. From above, Jun looks down on rows of faces angled toward the stage.
pages.transcript:
HOST
The high step is yours, Jun. Same as every opening singer before you.

JUN
From up here I can see everybody. Nobody can see anybody else.

pages.alt: Jun and Edda sit together at the edge of the market. Jun holds her red rosette, and Edda shows her a solitary blue button in her palm.
pages.transcript:
JUN
I practiced that solo all winter. I wanted the first note to be mine.

EDDA
Then spend it on something you’d miss. I’d miss the buttons lying down.

pages.alt: Jun holds out the red rosette across Edda’s worktable. Edda fixes it to the yellow pennant while the child steadies a corner.
pages.transcript:
JUN
Edda, will you take my opening bar? All of it. Even the knocking knees.

EDDA
I’ll borrow it. Here, let the back row have a corner.

pages.alt: Jun and the child stand in the open center of a circle of neighbors. The host rests his broad blue hat in his lap and smiles at the child.
pages.transcript:
JUN
Could we turn the rows into a ring? I’d rather see your faces.

HOST
Even mine? I suppose the hat can listen from down here.

pages.alt: The child watches between the baker’s loaf and the button seller’s tray. In front of the group, Edda raises one open hand and holds the rosette-trimmed pennant with the other.
pages.transcript:
CHILD
Is this the famous first note? I haven’t heard a thing.

EDDA
It’s my bit. Watch how long a harbor can hold its breath.

pages.alt: The baker pounds a rhythm on his bread board while the child joins in. The button seller tips her tin as an arch of envelopes and the sweeping yellow pennant echo the beat.
pages.transcript:
BAKER
One, two—BUN!

BUTTON SELLER
Hush now. Here come the buttons.

pages.alt: Jun sings from her place in the ring. In a wide view across the plaza, neighbors answer with lifted arms while Jun and Edda face one another under the swooping pennant.
pages.transcript:
JUN
Tin in the salt air, flour on the quay…

THE QUAY
How many songs can one harbor be?

pages.alt: Jun rests her cheek on her hand with a pencil over her book. Edda holds up a finished harbor print. Edda slides a blank sheet under Jun’s hand, and the pencil marks its first curve.
pages.transcript:
JUN
A new sound already? Scratch, hush. Scratch, hush. Whose is that?

EDDA
Yours. I left the back blank.
